# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

Cognitive science, like other experimental fields, has difficulty replicating its studies, making them transparent to readers, and verifying that they were run as planned [@osc2015; @nosek2022replicability; @hardwicke2018cognition; @claesen2021adherence]. Similar problems arise in data analysis and machine learning projects [@kapoor2023leakage]. We argued that a root cause of these problems is structural. A study's processes are spread across multiple separate documents (e.g., a registry entry, ethics documents, experiment code, analysis scripts, and figures drawn for publication), and because most of these documents are not machine-readable, ensuring quality, transparency, and replicability is arduous. In such conditions, documents are often incomplete, inaccurate, or outdated, and they drift apart, creating ambiguity and preventing verification and replication [@moher2010consort; @rennie2001].

The widely acknowledged need for better research practices has already changed how datasets are formatted, organized, and shared [@bids; @nwb2023; @psychds; @bdm]. What is critically missing, we argue, are better procedures for managing and documenting the *processes* involved in research. Studyflow, the solution presented in this paper, describes a study's processes in a single diagram that humans can understand and computers can execute. As demonstrated in this paper, this single diagram serves at once as the protocol, the runnable study, the data model, the analysis plan, the record of what was done, and the publication figures. Studyflow therefore provides a concrete and effective solution to several problems faced by current research practices.

## Key contributions of Studyflow to bettering cognitive science research

### Consistency: with one source there is nothing to drift

When each artifact carries its own copy of a study's parameters, the copies can drift apart, and information about the study becomes ambiguous, inaccurate, or wrong. Studyflow maintains only one file per study. The many documents that current practices produce, typically by hand, such as the participant flow, the study schedule, and checklists, serve different needs, sometimes of different stakeholders. Studyflow meets these needs while ensuring consistency, by replacing these documents with *views* generated from the information in the Studyflow diagram. This approach has further advantages. Generating views takes less effort and produces standardized outputs. Changing a study parameter automatically changes every view that uses it, so consistency holds by construction instead of depending on the effort of the authors.

### Sharing and replication: the study itself is shared, not a description of it

With Studyflow, a study is shared as one file in an open format. This file holds the diagram and its provenance as plain YAML text (or as metadata embedded in a TIFF, PNG, or SVG image), exports to standard BPMN, and is read by open source tools. Current practices instead share a collection of files, such as protocol documents, figures, and custom code, which can be hard to find, to open without proprietary software, and to read as one study. Such a collection may also include files the study never used and omit files it did use. A Studyflow diagram references every resource the protocol calls, such as the task software, the analysis functions, the data, and the consent form, and its provenance record shows which ones each run used, when, and how.

The Studyflow file and the resources it references together form the runnable study. A replicator can therefore open, validate, and rerun the study rather than reconstruct it from prose and code. Each task and analysis step names the program and version it calls, and the run record keeps the random seed and the execution environment [@w3cprov], so a rerun can use the same software as the original run [@peikert2021reproducible]. Even a figure exported from the diagram carries the whole diagram as embedded metadata, so a figure deposited with a paper is the study itself rather than a picture of it. Reproducibility thus becomes a property of the study artifact, rather than relying on voluntary practices with limited adoption [@hardwicke2024prevalence].

### Transparency: the coordination of a study is written down

A program both computes and coordinates its computations, setting their order, the conditions that decide which computation runs next, and the data each one uses [@gelernter1992coordination]. Studies that share code usually share the computations, such as a task or a statistical test, but leave the coordination implicit in function calls, shared variables, and undocumented decisions. A Studyflow diagram writes that coordination down. It draws and states the order of the steps, the conditions that select a path, the exclusions, and the data each step reads and writes. Writing them down exposes what prose leaves out. Once the study runs, Studyflow records exactly what was done, next to what was planned.

### Verifiability: checking a study no longer depends on reading the manuscript

Narrative reporting standards make verification costly and subjective, because assessing adherence means interpreting and comparing multiple non-standardized documents. Current recommendations ask authors to record by hand any deviations from their preregistrations [@willroth2024deviations]. This is time-consuming and error-prone, and undisclosed deviations are common [@goldacre2019compare; @claesen2021adherence; @hardwicke2023preregistration], even in a study that reported all of its analyses as preregistered [@bakcoleman2024rigour]. Large language models may help detect such deviations [@cummins2026regcheck], but their accuracy and trustworthiness remain to be established. In contrast, a Studyflow diagram is automatically verifiable. The validator checks that it is well-formed before any data are collected. The registered and the executed study are one file at two points in time, so a deviation shows up as a difference between them (@lst-diff). Each research question ends in a claim statement (e.g., "Supported", "Not supported", or "Not testable" in the example study) that its registered decision rule selects, with exclusions fixed before any data are collected [@simmons2011falsepositive]. This extends to the whole process what structured preregistration did for the plan [@peters2023preregr] and machine-readable hypothesis tests did for the claims [@lakens2021machinereadable].

Because any edit to the protocol changes the Studyflow file, the comparison detects every deviation by construction; its value lies in showing where each deviation was made and what it changed (@tbl-blind), much as version control systems do for code. Of course, this guarantee holds only if the registered diagram is deposited with a third party, such as a registry, where its authors cannot change it.

### A shared language across stakeholders

A study involves people with different backgrounds and interests. An ethics review panel needs the plan, an analyst needs to know where each dataset came from, a reviewer needs the participant flow, a replicator needs the whole study, and participants need to know what they agree to. Studyflow serves each of them through distinct views of the same diagram, in a form that the audience already knows, such as a schedule, a checklist, or a CONSORT flow diagram (@fig-views, panel B). Because the views share one source, their readers share one understanding of the study, even when each audience attends to different aspects of that study.

Studyflow supports this shared understanding by being a diagram that both humans and machines can read. Current practices rely on prose and code. Prose is accessible to most people but open to interpretation [@silberzahn2018manyanalysts; @botviniknezer2020variability]; code is unambiguous but does not serve all stakeholders well (e.g., not every member of an ethics review panel reads every programming language). In contrast, a Studyflow diagram is both accessible and unambiguous. It offers a picture of the study that non-technical readers can understand, and it contains structured plain text that technical experts can read, the validator can check, and the runner can execute. The picture and the text are two sides of the same coin. They describe the same study to every reader, in the form that suits each best. The diagram thus serves as a ubiquitous language for all stakeholders of the study [@ddd].

### Quality and efficiency: benefits arrive before publication

Studyflow can improve the quality of a study and make it more efficient to run, and these benefits arrive before any result is published. The validator checks the diagram for design faults, such as two decision criteria that overlap or an analysis that expects a data column the study will never store (@tbl-faults). The whole study, including its analysis, can then be simulated, to confirm that the analysis recovers what was built in (@tbl-planted). This extends the common advice to test a model on simulated data before collecting real data [@wilson2019tensimple] to the entire study. The figures common in publications, such as the participant flow diagram, are generated from the diagram rather than drawn by hand [@hopewell2025consort].

## Adopting Studyflow: the work involved

In the previous sections we listed various benefits of Studyflow for improving research practices. Here we briefly discuss how researchers can concretely adopt Studyflow, the hurdles they may face, and further benefits it may bring them personally.

### Software we provide

We developed open source tools to create, validate, and run Studyflow diagrams (<https://behaverse.org/studyflow>). The Studyflow Modeler is a web application that runs in the browser, also offline, in which researchers create and edit diagrams, inspect the provenance of past runs, and generate views such as a schedule, a checklist, and common reporting diagrams. A diagram is saved as YAML text, as BPMN 2.0 XML that other BPMN editors open, or as a PNG or SVG image that embeds the whole diagram and can be reopened for editing. The modeler also imports experiments defined in other task software, e.g., jsPsych timelines (the ordered lists of trials that jsPsych presents), and exports to further formats, such as draw.io and LinkML. Runners execute a diagram in a web browser or in a local environment, and a local run stores its outputs and logs in a Git repository. The modeler includes a gallery of example studies, and the documentation provides an overview of the notation, a reference, and notes for developers.

### Learning to use Studyflow

Using Studyflow requires learning a notation and the tools that read, write, and execute Studyflow diagrams. This takes some effort, but researchers are already familiar with many of the concepts involved, such as eligibility criteria, random allocation, exclusions, and flow diagrams. The tools and documentation described above support this learning, and further resources may be developed in the future. We believe the time invested will pay off quickly. The views remove the need to create several documents by hand, such as CONSORT flow diagrams, and Studyflow makes larger, more complex studies easier to manage, which is where current practices are particularly hard to maintain.

### How Studyflow relates to current research practices

Studyflow fits existing practices, because it calls the tools a study already uses rather than replacing them (@fig-overview). Experiment builders such as jsPsych [@deleeuw2015jspsych] and PsychoPy [@peirce2019psychopy] specify the trials, and workflow engines and workflow languages run and describe analysis pipelines at scale [@githubaction; @nextflow; @cwl]. None of these tools, however, expresses the experimental study as a whole. Studyflow fills this gap by describing the complete study and calling task code and analysis functions as individual steps. Studyflow also complements data standards [@bids; @psychds; @bdm] with a standardized description of the study processes [@aguilar2022experiments; @momeni2026guidelines] and could further enforce the use of data formats and standards.

### Practical benefits for researchers

Studyflow may facilitate specific steps of the research work. Instead of producing schedule diagrams or checklists manually, Studyflow offers means to generate these automatically. Studyflow may also facilitate discussing a study with collaborators by aligning everyone's understanding using one ubiquitous language rather than separate documents and scripts [@ddd]. Also, because the diagram is plain text, it works with version control systems, so changes to the diagram can be recorded, reviewed, and undone. Finally, the diagram supports data analysis. It links each dataset to a schema that serves as its data dictionary [@bdm], and the records of different platforms can be written to one shared dataset, aligned, for example, by participant, session, and time. Thus, we believe that Studyflow can provide direct benefits to researchers and practitioners from the start of a study's lifecycle.

## Limitations and future developments

The current version of Studyflow has obvious limitations. It is unclear, for example, whether all possible designs can be expressed in the notation. However, because Studyflow builds on BPMN and can further be extended, there would be options to address such cases as they arise (e.g., using another BPMN element or adding a new extension). Also, not everything in a study is necessarily best described as a Studyflow diagram. For example, the trial-level logic of a task may be better specified in a task builder.

While Studyflow itself is transparent and replicable, running a Studyflow diagram involves trusting the external software its activities reference. The run records what it can see of that software, such as its version, its environment, the arguments passed to it, and the number and classes of trials each task delivered, but whether a stimulus was shown as registered is beyond what validating the diagram can show. Studyflow could enforce good practices for such software, for example by requiring version-controlled code at a unique, persistent address, so that each reference from a diagram stays valid.

We have tested Studyflow with artificial agents. It has not yet been tested with human participants, and such studies may raise issues we have not anticipated. There are, however, no obvious reasons why Studyflow would not be able to handle such cases.

Finally, it is our belief that Studyflow diagrams are easier to read, write, and verify than the documents, figures, and scripts they replace. However, this has not been tested yet. Diagrams can make explicit the relations that a text leaves the reader to infer [@larkin1987diagram], but classic comparisons of flowcharts and text gave mixed results [@scanlan1989flowcharts; @shneiderman1977flowcharts]. Future studies should test these potential benefits [e.g., within usability studies, @figl2017comprehension] and possibly improve and extend various design aspects of Studyflow and its related applications (e.g., new elements, better icons, use of color, redesigning views).

## Conclusion

We believe Studyflow could be part of a new generation of research tools that scale up and improve experimental research in cognitive science and beyond. By giving the people and machines involved in a study one shared description of it, Studyflow eases their coordination, builds a shared understanding of the study, and increases its transparency and the trust in the validity of its results. As AI models become stakeholders in scientific studies [e.g., as research assistants or as participants, @dillion2023replace], these properties will let science take full advantage of these new opportunities without compromising rigor and trust.
